3. Skim [[001-Card Readers]] and [[002-Camera Placement]]. Most of our work starts there.

Folio shows the vault: a folder of pages that syncs to every PC. Staff read and comment in Folio. Contributors write in Obsidian, and an Administrator signs changes off in Review.

Open a page from Home, the sidebar, or search. Save the ones you come back to. What's New lists everything added or changed since you last looked.

# Submittal Review

> [!abstract] When to use this
> Every security submittal: product data, shop drawings, and samples. Allow five working days unless the contract says otherwise.

## Steps

1. **Log it.** Add the submittal to the project log the day it arrives, with the due date.
2. **Check it is complete.** Product data, shop drawings and the device schedule must all be there. If not, return it unreviewed.
3. **Review against the design.** Use [[004-Submittal Review Checklist]] and mark up the PDF.
4. **Pick the stamp.**
    - No exceptions taken
    - Make corrections noted
    - Revise and resubmit
    - Rejected
5. **Return it** through the project portal and update the log.

> [!warning] Do not approve substitutions here
> A product substitution needs the owner's written approval first. Return it as Revise and resubmit and say why.

## Stamps at a glance

| Stamp | Contractor can proceed | Resubmit needed |
|---|---|---|
| No exceptions taken | Yes | No |
| Make corrections noted | Yes, with the corrections | No |
| Revise and resubmit | No | Yes |
| Rejected | No | Yes, a new submittal |

## Reply text

> [!copy] Incomplete submittal
> This submittal is returned unreviewed because it is incomplete. Please resubmit with product data, shop drawings and the device schedule together.

# Commissioning Tests

## What we witness

Every door, camera and alarm point is tested once with the contractor present. We record pass or fail; we do not fix.

## Door tests

| Test | Expected | Pass when |
|---|---|---|
| Valid badge | Door unlocks, event logged | Both happen within 1 second |
| Invalid badge | Door stays locked, alarm logged | No unlock, event logged |
| Door held | Held alarm after 30 seconds | Alarm at the head end |
| Forced door | Forced alarm | Alarm immediately |
| Fire alarm release | Door unlocks on egress side | Unlocks, relocks on reset |

## Camera tests

- Image matches the field of view on the drawings
- Recording reaches the storage server
- Night image is usable at the darkest corner

> [!danger] Life safety comes first
> Never test a fire alarm release without the fire marshal's go-ahead and the building told.

# Card Readers

> [!abstract] Learning objectives
> - Explain why readers mount on the latch side.
> - Identify the right reader height for each door type.
> - Check a reader installation against the door schedule.

## Start here

![[reader-photo.png|inlR|240]]
A card reader is the device a person badges at to open a door. It sits on the **latch side**, where a hand naturally reaches, about 1.0 m above the floor. The reader on the secure side sets the height for both sides.

Most site problems are readers on the hinge side, or readers set at the height of the old light switch rather than the drawings.

### Latch side

The latch side is the side of the door that opens. A reader there is where the hand already is.

### Mounting height

Use 1.0 m to the centre of the reader unless the accessibility rules on [[003-Mounting Heights]] say lower.

## Going deeper

### Reader technology

| Type | Reads | Where we use it |
|---|---|---|
| Proximity, 125 kHz | Old badges only | Never on new work |
| Smart card, 13.56 MHz | Encrypted credentials | Standard for every door |
| Mobile | Phone credentials | Lobbies, by request |
| Biometric | Fingerprint or face | Data halls, second factor |

### Wiring

Run the reader cable home to the panel without a splice. Every splice is a fault waiting to happen.

## Worked example

Before and after on the same door: the first install put the reader on the hinge side.

![[before.png|320]] ![[after.png|320]]
*Left: hinge side, as found. Right: moved to the latch side.*

## What to check on a site walk

- Reader on the latch side
- Centre at 1.0 m, or lower where the schedule says
- Cover plate fitted and no cable showing

## Check yourself

> [!question]- Why does the secure side set the height?
> Because both readers on a door should match, and the secure side is the one that must meet accessibility.

> [!question]- What reader type goes on new work?
> Smart card, 13.56 MHz.

# Camera Placement

> [!abstract] Learning objectives
> - Choose a camera position from what the picture must show.
> - Avoid backlight and glare at doors.

## Start here

![[rack.png|inlL|240]]
A camera is placed for the question someone will ask later: who came through this door, and when. Start from the picture you need, then find the spot that gives it.

Put cameras at doors facing in, not out, so faces are lit by the room rather than the sky.

## Coverage levels

| Level | Can you | Use at |
|---|---|---|
| Detect | Tell something moved | Fence lines |
| Observe | See what a person is doing | Corridors |
| Recognise | Know someone you have met | Inside doors |
| Identify | Pick out a stranger | Entry points |

## Mistakes we see

> [!warning] Backlight
> A camera facing a glass door at noon shows a black shape. Move it or use a wide dynamic range camera.

- Mounted too high to see faces
- Pointed at a wall that was going to be a hallway
- Lens set to the wrong field of view after a layout change

## Worked example

The Dallas lobby has a glass wall facing west. The first design put the entry camera on the far wall, looking out, and every afternoon it showed silhouettes. Moving it beside the door, looking in, gave usable faces all day.

> [!example] What changed
> Camera moved from the far wall to the door frame, aimed into the lobby. Lens narrowed to the turnstile line.

# Door Hardware Basics

## Start here

A secure door is a set of parts working together: the lock, the strike, a door position switch, and a way out. We specify the security parts; the hardware consultant specifies the rest.

## Locks

| Lock | Fails | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Electric strike | Secure or safe | Office doors |
| Electrified lockset | Secure | Most interior doors |
| Magnetic lock | Safe | Only where code allows |

## Egress

> [!danger] Free egress always
> People must always be able to leave. Every secured door needs a way out that does not depend on our system.

# Intrusion Detection

## Start here

Intrusion detection tells us when someone is somewhere they should not be, when the area is armed. The panel groups sensors into zones and areas.

## Sensors

- Door contacts on every perimeter door
- Motion sensors in rooms with windows
- Glass break where glass is reachable from outside

## Zones and areas

An area is what you arm and disarm. A zone is one sensor or a small group of them. Name zones by room number, never by what the room is used for today.

> [!tip] Test from the panel
> Walk test every zone with the panel in test mode. The report is your proof.

# Cable Pathways

## Start here

Security cable runs in its own pathway from the device to the panel. Sharing with other trades causes the faults we spend days chasing.

## Rules

1. Conduit from the device box to above the ceiling.
2. Cable tray or J-hooks above the ceiling, every 1.2 m.
3. Conduit again into the security room.

## In the rack

![[before.png|inlR|240]]
Dress cable in the rack with velcro, never cable ties, and label both ends. A rack you can trace is a rack you can fix.

Leave a service loop at the panel, not at the device. Three metres is enough for a panel move inside the room.

# Travel and Expenses

> [!abstract] When to use this
> Any trip for a project or for training, and any money you spend for the firm. For site safety and what to pack, see [[003-Site Travel]].

## Steps

1. **Get the trip approved.** Your project lead approves the dates and the project code before anything is booked.
2. **Book through the travel desk.** Use the [travel booking tool](https://example.com/travel). It applies the firm's rates and keeps your itinerary in one place.
3. **Keep every receipt.** A photo on your phone is enough. Lost receipts need a short note signed by your lead.
4. **Claim within 30 days.** Enter the claim in the [expense portal](https://example.com/expenses) with the project code on every line.
5. **Your lead approves, Finance pays.** Most claims are paid in the next pay run.

> [!warning] Claims older than 60 days
> Finance cannot pay them without a director's sign-off. Claim as soon as you are back.

## What the firm covers

| Item | Covered | Notes |
|---|---|-------------|
| Flights | Economy | Book at least 14 days out where you can |
| Hotel | Standard room | Near the site, from the travel tool's list |
| Meals | Daily allowance | Set by Finance each year, shown in the portal |
| Mileage | Per mile rate | Your own car only, from the office or home, whichever is shorter |
| Rental car | Compact | Add the firm's insurance at the counter |

## Project codes

Every line of a claim needs a project code. The format is always the same:

```
PRJ-<year>-<number>-<task>
PRJ-2026-0142-TRV
```

Task **TRV** is travel, **TRN** is training, **GEN** is anything else.

## Describing a claim

Paste this into the description field and fill in the brackets:

> [!copy] Claim description
> Site visit to [site name] for [project name], [dates]. Approved by [lead].

## Who to ask

Finance answers expense questions. See [[004-Who to Ask]] for the right person.

# IT Help and Tools

## Getting help

Most problems are fixed fastest through the [help desk portal](https://example.com/helpdesk). Call only if you cannot sign in at all.

> [!tip] A good help request
> Say what you were doing, what you expected, and what happened instead. A screenshot saves a round trip.

Use this subject line so the request reaches the right team:

```
[Laptop | Account | Software | Phone] short description
Example: [Software] drawing viewer will not open PDFs
```

## The everyday tools

| Tool | What it is for | Where |
|---|---|------------|
| Folio | How we work: processes, guides, policies, people | You are here |
| Email and calendar | Day-to-day communication | [Web mail](https://example.com/mail) |
| Chat and meetings | Quick questions, calls, screen sharing | [Chat app](https://example.com/chat) |
| Document system | Contracts, drawings and anything formally issued | [Documents](https://example.com/docs) |
| Timesheets | Hours, by project code | [Timesheets](https://example.com/timesheets) |
| Expenses | Travel and spending claims | [Expense portal](https://example.com/expenses) |

> [!note] Folio is not the document system
> Folio explains how to do the work and points to the systems you do it in. Contracts, drawings and anything formally issued stay in the document system, under document control. See [[002-Document Control]].

## Passwords and accounts

- Change your password every 90 days; the system reminds you.
- Never share an account. Ask IT for a shared mailbox instead.
- Lost a laptop or phone? Call the help desk straight away, day or night.

## New software

Ask your lead first, then raise a **[Software]** request. IT checks licences and security before anything is installed.

# Our Project Lifecycle

> [!abstract] When to use this
> To see where a project is, what comes next, and which page explains the steps. Each phase links to its own process.

![[lifecycle.png]]
*Five phases. The blue ones have a step-by-step process page in Folio.*

## 1. Win the work

The proposal, the fee and the team. Leadership signs off the fee before it goes out. The signed contract goes into the [document system](https://example.com/docs), not into Folio.

## 2. Design the job

Drawings and specifications, with internal reviews before each issue.

- Review checklist: [[004-Submittal Review Checklist]]
- Standards we design to: [[002-Standards Library]]

## 3. Build on site

The contractor builds; we review what they submit and walk the site.

- [[001-Submittal Review]]
- [[002-Site Walk]]

## 4. Test and prove

Every device tested against the design before the owner accepts it.

- [[003-Commissioning Tests]]

## 5. Close and hand over

As-built records, warranties and training, handed to the owner in one package.

- [[005-Closeout Package]]

> [!note] One process, many groups
> Every design group follows the same five phases. Each group writes its own process pages for the parts that differ, and links them here, so anyone can follow a project from start to finish.

> [!question]- Where do contracts and official forms live?
> In the [document system](https://example.com/docs), under document control. Folio explains how to do the work and links to the official copy, so there is only ever one version of the real thing.

section-order: in order

use-for: teaching one subject so a new person can work on site and a designer can go deeper.
not-for: steps for one job (use Process) or facts people look up (use Reference).
%%

# {{title}}

> [!abstract] Learning objectives
> - [Explain …]
> - [Identify …]
> - [Check …]

%% Callout · Core · Expects: callout (summary), bullet list. Three to five objectives, each starting with a verb: what the reader can do when finished. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Writing a Guide page
> A Guide teaches **one subject**. Picture a new starter on their first site visit, and a designer who needs the detail. The page should work for both: the first sections for the new starter, the later ones for the designer.
>
> **How a Guide is laid out**
>
> | Section | Who it serves | Keep it to |
> | :-- | :-- | :------- |
> | Learning objectives | Everyone | Three to five lines |
> | Start here | The new starter | What it is and why it matters |
> | Going deeper | The designer | Standards, numbers, edge cases |
> | Worked example or Field scenarios | Both | One real case, start to finish |
> | What to check on a site walk | The person on site | Only things you can see or test |
> | Check yourself | The learner | Three to six questions |
> | References | Anyone going further | Pages first, then standards |
>
> **Writing the objectives**
>
> Start each with a verb a trainer could test: Explain, Identify, Check, Choose, Mount. Not "Understand" or "Know about".
>
> ```md
> - Explain why readers mount on the latch side.
> - Identify the right reader height for each door type.
> - Check a reader installation against the door schedule.
> ```
>
> > [!tip] One subject per page
> > If the objectives cover two subjects, it is two Guides. Link them from each other's References.

## Start here

%% Core · Expects: text, picture. The core idea in plain words. A new reader can stop here and still be useful. One picture beside the text. %%

![[diagram-name.png|inlR|240]]
[Write the core idea in two or three short paragraphs. Say what it is, why it matters on site, and the one thing people get wrong.]

> [!guide]- Guide: Start here
> This is the most read section of the page. Many readers stop here, so it must stand on its own.
>
> **Good**
>
> A card reader is the device a person badges at to open a door. It sits on the **latch side**, where a hand naturally reaches, 1.0 m above the floor. The reader on the secure side sets the height for both sides.
>
> **Do**
> - Use one picture beside the text: a photo of the thing, or a simple diagram.
> - Keep it to what a new starter needs on day one.
>
> **Don't**
> - Don't start with history or standards. Those belong in Going deeper.
> - Don't use a term you have not explained.

### Key idea

%% Core · Repeat. One heading per key idea, two to four in total. Rename each heading to the idea itself. %%

[Explain one key idea in a short paragraph. Rename this heading.]

> [!guide]- Guide: Key ideas
> Break the subject into two to four ideas a new starter must hold on to. Each gets its own sub-section, named for the idea: "Latch side", "Mounting height", "Secure side sets the rules".
>
> ```md
> ### Latch side
> ### Mounting height
> ```
>
> Rename this heading, then copy it (heading, note and text) for each further idea.

## Going deeper

%% Core · Expects: text, callout (warning). Specifications, standards and numbers. Name each standard with its edition. %%

[Write the detail a designer needs: specifications, standards, numbers and exceptions.]

> [!warning] Common mistake
> [What people get wrong, and how to avoid it.]

> [!guide]- Guide: Going deeper
> This is the designer's section. Numbers, standards, the reasons behind the rules, and the exceptions.
>
> - Name every standard with its edition: "NFPA 101, 2024 edition".
> - Use a table when comparing options or door types.
> - Keep one **warning** callout for the mistake people really make. Delete it if there is none.
>
> > [!tip] Link, don't repeat
> > If another page already explains a detail, link to it instead of copying it. Copies go out of date.

### Sub-topic

%% Core · Repeat. One heading per sub-topic of the detail. Rename each heading. %%

[Write one sub-topic. Rename this heading.]

## Worked example

%% One of: practice · Expects: table (Input, Value, Source). One real calculation or decision, start to finish. A page needs this, Field scenarios, or both. %%

| Input | Value | Source |
| :-- | :-- | :------- |
| [Input] | [Value] | [Where it comes from] |

**Answer:** [The result, and what it means.]

> [!guide]- Guide: Worked example or Field scenarios
> A Guide needs at least one of these two sections. Keep one, or both, and delete the other.
>
> - **Worked example** suits a calculation or a design choice: inputs, the working, the answer.
> - **Field scenarios** suit site work: what you find, what it means, what you do.
>
> | Input | Value | Source |
> | :-- | :-- | :------- |
> | Door width | 915 mm | Door schedule, D-101 |
> | Reader offset from frame | 150 mm | Standard detail SD-04 |
>
> **Answer:** The reader centre sits 150 mm from the latch-side frame, 1.0 m above the floor.

## Field scenarios

%% One of: practice · Expects: table (You find, It means, You do). Two to four site situations and what to do in each. %%

| You find | It means | You do |
| :-- | :-- | :------- |
| [What you see on site] | [Why it matters] | [The action to take] |

## What to check on a site walk

%% Core · Expects: tick list. Only things you can see, touch or test, in the order you walk them. %%

- [ ] [Something you can see or test]
- [ ] [Something you can see or test]

> [!guide]- Guide: Site walk
> Write it for someone standing at the door with this page on a phone.
>
> - [ ] Reader is on the latch side.
> - [ ] Reader is 1.0 m above the finished floor.
> - [ ] Tamper screws are fitted.
>
> **Don't** list things nobody can check on a walk, such as "configured correctly".

## Check yourself

%% Core · Expects: numbered list, callout (question). Three to six questions. The answers go in the folded callout so readers try first. %%

1. [A question]
2. [A question]
3. [A question]

> [!question]- Answers
> 1. [Answer]
> 2. [Answer]
> 3. [Answer]

> [!guide]- Guide: Check yourself
> Ask about the learning objectives, one question each. Keep the numbering of the answers the same as the questions.
>
> The minus sign in `> [!question]-` keeps the answers folded, so readers try before they look.

## References

%% Core · Expects: link · Was: Sources. Linked pages first, then standards with edition and year. %%

- [[Page name]]
- [Standard, edition and year]

## Video

%% Optional · Was: Videos. Only when a good video exists. Delete the heading if not. %%

- [Video title](https://)

> 1. Confirm the backing is in place before drywall.
> 2. Mount the reader on the latch side, 1.0 m above the floor.
> 	1. Level it.
> 	2. Fix it with tamper screws.
> 3. Request the test from the security subcontractor.
>
> - Sub-steps indent with Tab. Two levels at most.
> - A picture under a step is fine when it saves words. Add a caption line.
>
> **Don't** hide a warning inside a step. Put it in Common mistakes, or a warning callout straight after the step.

# {{title}}

> [!abstract] Summary
> This page shows every part a Folio page can use: headings, text, links, lists, tables, pictures, callouts and more. Each part comes with an example, what to type, and a short do and don't list.

%% Callout · Core · Expects: callout (summary). Most templates open with one callout straight under the title: objectives for a Guide, key facts for a Reference. Keep it and rename its title for the new type. %%

## Start here

%% Core. Template builders: delete this section. It only teaches. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Start here
> Folio is where the team **reads**. Obsidian is where you **write**. Every page is a plain text file, so what you type in Obsidian is exactly what Folio shows.
>
> **Three things to know before you start**
>
> 1. **Replace everything in [square brackets].** Brackets mark starter text. The format check in Vault check lists any page that still has some.
> 2. **Grey text and purple Guide boxes are for editors only.** Folio never shows them. Grey notes say what goes in a section; delete them once done. Guide boxes teach, like this one; leave them folded and they stay out of your way.
> 3. **Keep the headings the template gives you.** You can add sub-sections. If you rename or remove a main section, the page no longer matches its template, and Vault check will point it out.
>
> > [!tip] Work side by side
> > Keep Folio open on this page while you write in Obsidian. Folio shows the finished look. Obsidian shows what to type.
>
> **The five-minute version**
>
> - [ ] Start the page from **+ New page** in Folio, not from Obsidian.
> - [ ] Fill in the **summary** property with one sentence.
> - [ ] Write each section, replacing the [brackets].
> - [ ] Add pictures with a caption line under each.
> - [ ] Delete the grey notes when you are done.
> - [ ] Folio shows the page as **In review** until an Admin approves it.

## The parts of a page

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: The parts of a page
> Every page has the same five parts, in this order.
>
> | Part | Where it is | What it holds | Who fills it |
> | :-- | :-- | :-- | :------- |
> | Properties | The very top, between two lines of three dashes | Facts about the page: type, number, status, dates | Mostly Folio. You fill summary and tags |
> | Title | The one line starting with a single # | The page name. It matches the file name, without the number | Folio, from New page |
> | Opening callout | Straight under the title | A summary, objectives or key facts | You |
> | Sections | Headings starting with ## | The body of the page | You |
> | References | The last section | Pages and standards the page relies on | You |

## Properties

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section. The property block at the top of the file is set by Folio for every template. Do not add or remove properties. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Properties
> Properties are the block at the very top of the file. Obsidian shows it as a small form. Folio fills most of them for you. **You only fill in summary and tags.**
>
> | Property | Who fills it | What it means | Example |
> | :-- | :-- | :------- | :-- |
> | type | Folio | Which template the page follows | guide |
> | summary | **You** | One sentence, 160 characters or fewer. It shows under the title and in search | How card readers are mounted and tested at data hall doors. |
> | number | Folio | The page's three-digit number in its top folder | 021 |
> | tags | **You** | A few topic words, lower case, hyphens between words | access-control, readers |
> | aliases | You, if needed | Other names people search for | ACR, card reader |
> | status | Folio | To Be Reviewed, or Reviewed once an Admin approves | To Be Reviewed |
> | reviewed | Folio | The date an Admin approved the page | 2026-09-27 |
> | created | Folio | The date the page was made | 2026-09-27 |
> | due | Admin | A date the page must be finished by, if any | 2026-10-15 |
> | author | Folio | Who started the page | Jayson Stickrod |
> | edited-by, edited-at | Folio | Who changed it last, and when | |
> | must-read, must-read-start | Admin | Whether everyone must read it, and from when | false |
> | onboarding, onboarding-due | Admin | Whether new staff must read it, and by when | false |
>
> > [!warning] Leave the property names alone
> > Change what comes after the colon, never the word before it. A misspelled property name is a new, empty property, and Folio will not find the real one.
>
> **Do**
> - Write the summary as a sentence a reader would want to see in search results.
> - Use the same tags other pages use. Check an existing page first.
>
> **Don't**
> - Don't type status or reviewed yourself. Review sets them.
> - Don't paste a paragraph into summary.

## File names and numbers

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: File names and numbers
> Every file name is **a three-digit number, a hyphen, then the title**, for example `021-Intrusion Detection.md`.
>
> - The number is unique inside its **top folder**. So 20_Guides and 10_Processes can both have a 021.
> - New page shows the next free number, and you can change it. A number that is already taken is flagged.
> - A new page waits in **00_Home / Working Drafts** until it is approved, then it moves to its folder.
> - Folio never renames a page. Rename it in Obsidian, so every link to it follows.
>
> **Don't**
> - Don't use two digits (`21-`) or four (`0021-`).
> - Don't use these characters in a title: `\ / : * ? " < > | # ^ [ ]`. They break file names or links.

## Headings

%% Core · Expects: heading levels. Every template needs at least two Core sections. Template builders: keep the rule text and delete the examples. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Headings
> Headings split a page into parts a reader can jump to, from the outline on the right in Folio.
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> # The page title (only one, Folio writes it)
> ## A section
> ### A sub-section inside it
> #### A deeper level (only if the template allows it)
> ```
>
> - Use **## for sections** and **### for sub-sections**. Most pages need nothing deeper.
> - #### is available only where Format rules or the template allow it. The house default stops at ###.
> - Keep headings short, six words or fewer, in sentence case: "Mounting heights", not "Mounting Heights For All Doors".
>
> > [!tip] Rename carefully
> > Links can point at a heading (see Links). If you rename a heading, links to it break. The template's grey note says what the heading used to be called (was), so Folio can still match older pages.
>
> **Do**
> - One idea per section.
> - Add sub-sections freely under a section marked Repeat.
>
> **Don't**
>
> ```md
> ## 1. Scope            (no numbers: they break when sections move)
> ## **Scope**           (no bold in headings)
> ## Scope of Work.      (no full stop)
> ##### Detail           (too deep: split the page instead)
> ## See [[Card Readers]] (no links in headings)
> ```

### A sub-section

%% Optional · Repeat. Repeat means writers can add as many headings at this level as they need, each with its own name. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Headings
> This is a sub-section. It belongs to the section above it. In a template, a sub-section marked Repeat usually has a placeholder name like "Key idea", which the writer renames.

#### A deeper level

%% Optional. Only in templates whose deepest heading is H4 or more (set in Format rules). Delete it everywhere else. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Headings
> Use a fourth level only when a sub-section really splits in two. If you reach for a fifth, the page is doing too much. Split it into two pages and link them.

## Writing text

%% Core. Every template has plain text somewhere. Template builders: delete the examples and keep one line of [starter text]. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Writing text
> Write the way you would explain it to a new colleague on site: short paragraphs, plain words, one idea at a time.
>
> Card readers mount on the **latch side** of the door, 1.0 m above the finished floor. The reader on the secure side sets the height for both.
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> Card readers mount on the **latch side** of the door, 1.0 m above the finished floor.
> ```
>
> - **Bold** one key term per paragraph at most, so it stands out.
> - Spell out an acronym the first time: access control panel (ACP), then ACP.
> - Keep paragraphs to about 120 words. Format rules flag longer ones.
> - Put a blank line between paragraphs. Obsidian keeps the line breaks you type, and so does Folio.
>
> **Don't**
>
> ```md
> ==highlighted text==      (no highlight: use a callout instead)
> <u>underlined</u>         (no underline: it looks like a link)
> ~~struck out~~            (no strikethrough: delete it, the change log keeps history)
> *italic for emphasis*     (italics are only for picture captions)
> ```

## Links

%% Optional · Expects: link. Template builders: keep this section only if the new type links to other pages outside References. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Links
> Links join pages together. They are what turn separate pages into a wiki.
>
> Hardware sets are in [[Door Hardware Schedule]]. Mounting heights are in [[Card Readers#Mounting heights]]. The maker's guide is [on their site](https://example.com).
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> [[Door Hardware Schedule]]                     a page in the vault
> [[Door Hardware Schedule|the hardware sets]]   the same page, with your own words
> [[Card Readers#Mounting heights]]              a section of a page
> [on their site](https://example.com)           a web page, with words
> ```
>
> > [!tip] Type two square brackets
> > In Obsidian, type `[[` and start the page name. It suggests pages as you type, and keeps links working when a page is renamed.
>
> **Do**
> - Link the first time you mention another page, not every time.
> - Use words that say where the link goes.
>
> **Don't**
>
> ```md
> https://example.com/specs.pdf       (bare web address: give it words)
> Click [[here|Card Readers]]         (click here: say what it is)
> ```

## Lists

%% Optional · Expects: bullet list, numbered list, tick list. Template builders: keep the one list type the new section needs and delete the others. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Lists
> There are three kinds of list. Pick by what the reader will do with it.
>
> **Bullets: when order does not matter**
>
> - Single doors
> - Double doors
> 	- Active leaf only
> - Mantrap doors
>
> **Numbers: when order matters**
>
> 1. Confirm the backing is in place.
> 2. Mount the reader.
> 	1. Level it.
> 	2. Fix it with tamper screws.
> 3. Terminate and test.
>
> **Tick boxes: things to check**
>
> - [ ] Reader height is 1.0 m.
> - [ ] Tamper switch works.
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> - A bullet
> 	- A bullet under it (press Tab first)
> 1. A step
> 	1. A sub-step (press Tab first)
> - [ ] Something to check
> - [x] Something checked
> ```
>
> **Do**
> - Start each step with a verb: Mount, Check, Send.
> - Keep to two levels. Tab indents a level, Shift and Tab goes back one.
>
> **Don't**
> - Don't nest three levels deep. Split it into a new section instead.
> - Don't use tick boxes for ordinary lists. They mean "check this".

## Tables

%% Optional · Expects: table. Template builders: keep a table only where pages compare things side by side. Set its columns and give the Notes column room. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Tables
> Tables compare things side by side. The line of dashes under the header does more than it looks: it sets how wide each column is.
>
> **A table sized to its content** (three dashes per column)
>
> | Door type | Height | Side |
> | :-- | :-- | :-- |
> | Single | 1.0 m | Latch |
> | Accessible | 0.9 m | Push button |
>
> **A table with room for notes** (four or more dashes give a column room)
>
> | Door type | Height | Notes |
> | :-- | :-- | :------- |
> | Single | 1.0 m | Standard mounting, no backing plate needed |
> | Cage door | 1.1 m | Fix to a mesh backing plate so the reader cannot be pushed in |
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> | Door type | Height | Notes    |
> | :--       | :--    | :------- |
> | Single    | 1.0 m  | Standard |
> ```
>
> - `:--` keeps text on the left. `--:` puts numbers on the right. `:-:` centres.
> - Folio pins the header row as you scroll a long table.
> - For a schedule that needs the whole page width, put the word wide between double percent signs on the line straight above the table. It then runs margin to margin.
>
> > [!tip] Let Obsidian draw it
> > In Obsidian, right-click an empty line and pick Insert > Table. Tab moves to the next cell, and Enter adds a row. You never need to line the bars up yourself.
>
> **Do**
> - Always have a header row.
> - Put units in the header (Height, m) or next to every value, the same all the way down.
>
> **Don't**
> - Don't go past six columns unless the table is marked wide.
> - Don't put pictures, lists or line breaks inside a cell.
> - Don't use a picture of a table. Type it, so search can find it.

## Pictures

%% Optional · Expects: picture. Template builders: keep one picture layout per section at most. Full width suits drawings, beside the text suits photos, side by side suits before and after. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Pictures
> Drag a picture into Obsidian, or paste it. Obsidian saves the file in the vault's attachments folder and adds the line for you. Then add what you want after the file name.
>
> **Full width, with a caption** (drawings and plans)
>
> ![[sample-level1-plan.png]]
> *Figure 1. Level 1 data halls, reader doors marked in red.*
>
> **Beside the text** (photos)
>
> ![[sample-reader-photo.png|inlR|240]]
> The reader sits on the latch side of the door. The picture floats to the right and this paragraph wraps beside it, then carries on underneath once it runs past the bottom. Use inlL instead to put the picture on the left. Pick a width from three sizes: 180 small, 240 medium, 320 large.
>
> **Side by side** (before and after)
>
> ![[sample-before.png|320]] ![[sample-after.png|320]]
> *Figure 2. The same cabinet before and after the cabling was dressed.*
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> ![[plan.png]]
> *Figure 1. What the drawing shows.*
>
> ![[photo.png|inlR|240]]
> Text that wraps beside it.
>
> ![[before.png|320]] ![[after.png|320]]
> *Figure 2. Before and after.*
> ```
>
> - The **caption** is an italic line straight under the picture, starting with Figure and a number.
> - Name the file for what it shows: `reader-latch-side.png`, not `IMG_4471.png`.
>
> **Don't**
> - Don't use a screenshot of text. Type the text.
> - Don't leave a picture without a caption. Format rules flag it.
> - Don't make a picture beside the text wider than 320. The text next to it gets too narrow to read.

## Callouts

%% Optional · Expects: callout. Template builders: keep only the callout kinds the new type uses, one meaning each. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Callouts
> A callout is a coloured box that makes one thing stand out. There are seven kinds, and **each one means one thing**, so readers learn the colours once.
>
> | Kind | Type this | Use it for | Colour |
> | :-- | :-- | :------- | :-- |
> | Summary | `> [!abstract]` | Objectives, key facts, the short version | Teal |
> | Note | `> [!note]` | Background or an exception | Blue |
> | Tip | `> [!tip]` | A faster or better way | Teal |
> | Warning | `> [!warning]` | A common mistake and how to avoid it | Orange |
> | Danger | `> [!danger]` | A safety or security risk only | Red |
> | Copy | `> [!copy]` | Text people paste elsewhere. Folio adds a Copy button | Grey |
> | Question | `> [!question]-` | Answers, folded so readers try first | Orange |
>
> **How they look**
>
> > [!abstract] Key facts
> > Readers mount at 1.0 m on the latch side.
>
> > [!note]
> > Older buildings may use 1.1 m. Match the existing doors on the same floor.
>
> > [!tip] Faster testing
> > Test all readers on one panel in a single visit.
>
> > [!warning] Common mistake
> > Never test with the door wedged open. The door contact never changes state.
>
> > [!danger] Security risk
> > Removing the tamper switch disables the alarm for the whole door.
>
> > [!copy] Standard reply
> > Thanks for the drawings. We will review them and reply by [date].
>
> > [!question]- Answers
> > 1. On the latch side.
> > 2. 1.0 m above the finished floor.
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> > [!warning] Common mistake
> > Never test with the door wedged open.
>
> > [!question]- Answers
> > A minus sign after the kind starts it folded.
> ```
>
> **Do**
> - Give a callout a short title after the kind, or leave it blank to use the kind's name.
> - One callout per point. Two warnings in a row is fine. Five means the section needs rewriting.
>
> **Don't**
> - Don't use danger for things that are merely important.
> - Don't put a callout inside another callout.
> - Don't use kinds outside the seven, such as bug or example. They look different in Folio and Obsidian.

## Copy text

%% Optional · Expects: callout (copy). Keep it where pages hold emails, letters or form text that people paste somewhere else. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Copy text
> When people need exact words to paste into an email or a form, put them in a Copy callout. Folio adds a Copy button, so nobody has to select text by hand.
>
> > [!copy] Request for access
> > Please add [name] to the [site] access list for [dates]. Their badge number is [number].
>
> - Mark what changes in [square brackets], so the reader knows what to replace.

## Code and exact settings

%% Optional · Expects: code. Keep it only where pages give commands or settings that must be typed exactly. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Code and exact settings
> Use a code block for anything that must be typed exactly: commands, settings, addresses. Folio shows it in a fixed-width font with a Copy button.
>
> ```powershell
> Get-Service -Name "AccessControl*"
> ```
>
> **What you type**
>
> ````md
> ```powershell
> Get-Service -Name "AccessControl*"
> ```
> ````
>
> - Name the language after the three backticks: powershell, bash, json, yaml, or text.
> - The format check skips code blocks. That is why this page can show don'ts inside them.

## Quotes from a standard

%% Optional · Expects: quote. Keep it where pages quote codes or standards word for word. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Quotes from a standard
> Quote a standard only when the exact wording matters, and say where it came from.
>
> > "Doors shall be arranged to be opened readily from the egress side whenever the building is occupied."
> > NFPA 101, 7.2.1.5.1, 2024 edition
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> > "The exact words."
> > Standard, clause, edition
> ```
>
> - A quote is a greater-than sign with no kind in brackets. With a kind, it becomes a callout.

## How Folio reads a template

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section from new templates. It is the reference for everything Folio relies on. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: How Folio reads a template
> A template is an ordinary Markdown file in `zSystem/Templates/`. Folio reads six things from it. If one of them is missing or misspelled, Folio falls back to the default shown here, and Vault check says so.
>
> **1. Template settings** (the header note at the very top)
>
> | Setting | What it controls | Values | Default |
> | :-- | :------- | :-- | :-- |
> | name | The name on the Templates tab and in New page | Any short name | The file name |
> | version | Goes up by one each time the sections change. Vault check compares pages to the version they were made from | 1, 2, 3 | 1 |
> | type | The value written to a new page's type property | Lower case, one word | name, lower case |
> | offer-in-new-page | Whether writers can pick it in New page | yes, no | yes |
> | usual-folder | The top folder New page suggests, and where the number comes from | A top folder, or none | none |
> | starting-tags | Tags a new page starts with | Words separated by commas | none |
> | section-order | Whether sections must stay in this order | in order, any order | in order |
> | extra-sections | Whether a page may add sections the template does not have | flagged, allowed | flagged |
> | deepest-heading | The deepest heading a page may use. Overrides Format rules for this type | H2 to H6 | Format rules |
> | use-for | One sentence shown in New page | Text | none |
> | not-for | One sentence shown in New page | Text | none |
>
> **2. Headings.** Every `##`, `###` and `####` is a section of the Outline, in order. Names must be unique in the file.
>
> **3. Badges.** The grey note straight under a heading starts with its badges, separated by a middle dot, ending with a full stop. See "Notes for editors" for the full list. Only the first sentence is read; the rest is guidance for the writer.
>
> ```md
> %% Core · Repeat · Expects: numbered list · Was: Method. One action per step. %%
> ```
>
> **4. Expects.** The shapes a section should hold. Folio checks the shape is there, never what it says.
>
> | Write | Means |
> | :-- | :-- |
> | text | At least one paragraph |
> | bullet list, numbered list, tick list | That kind of list |
> | table | Any table |
> | table (Item, Value, Notes) | A table with these header names |
> | picture | At least one picture, with a caption |
> | callout | Any callout |
> | callout (warning) | A callout of that kind |
> | code, code (powershell) | A code block, of that language |
> | quote | A quote |
> | link | At least one link |
>
> List several with commas: `Expects: numbered list, callout (warning)`.
>
> **5. Stand-ins.** `{{title}}` and `{{date}}` are filled by New page. Anything in [square brackets] is starter text the writer must replace. Vault check finds it.
>
> **6. Special blocks.**
>
> | Block | Folio | New page | Approve |
> | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
> | Header note (settings) | Read, never shown | Removed | |
> | Grey note under a heading | Read for badges, never shown | Kept | Removed if ticked |
> | Guide box (`> [!guide]-`) | Never shown | Kept | Removed if ticked |
> | Word wide between double percent signs above a table | Table runs margin to margin | Kept | Kept |
>
> > [!warning] Check it on the Outline tab
> > After saving a template in Obsidian, open it on Folio's Outline tab. If a badge is misspelled, the Outline shows it without a badge and Vault check lists the template.

## Notes for editors

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section. It explains the grey notes you are reading. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Notes for editors
> Grey notes are text between two pairs of percent signs. Obsidian shows them grey while you edit. Folio never shows them. They are for the people writing the page, not the people reading it.
>
> **What you type**
>
> ```md
> %% Anything here is for editors only. %%
> ```
>
> In a **template**, the note straight under each heading is special. It starts with its **badges**, then says what to write. Folio reads the badges to build the template's Outline, and the format check uses them.
>
> | Badge | Type this at the start of the note | Means |
> | :-- | :-- | :------- |
> | core | `Core` | Every page of this type has this section |
> | optional | `Optional` | Leave it out if there is nothing for it |
> | one of | `One of: practice` | A page needs at least one section from the named group |
> | repeat | `Repeat` | Writers can add as many of these headings as they need |
> | callout | `Callout` | The callout straight under the title |
> | Expects | `Expects: table (Item, Value, Notes)` | The shape the section should hold |
> | was | `Was: Sources` | The heading's old name, so older pages still match |
>
> Separate badges with a middle dot and spaces, then end with a full stop:
>
> ```md
> %% Core · Repeat · Expects: numbered list. One action per step. %%
> ```
>
> **Don't**
> - Don't put two percent signs inside a note. It ends the note early, and the rest shows on the page.
> - Don't leave notes on a finished page. Vault check lists reviewed pages that still have them.

## Placeholders and starter text

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Placeholders and starter text
> Templates use two kinds of stand-in text.
>
> | Kind | Looks like | Who replaces it |
> | :-- | :-- | :-- |
> | Placeholder | `{{title}}`, `{{date}}` | Folio, when it creates the page |
> | Starter text | `[Write the core idea here.]` | You, while writing |
>
> - Starter text always sits in square brackets, so it is easy to spot and the format check can find it.
> - Write starter text as an instruction: "[List what to check on a site walk.]", not "[Text]".

## Not used on Folio pages

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Not used on Folio pages
> Obsidian can do more than Folio shows well. These are left out on purpose.
>
> | Not used | Why | Use instead |
> | :-- | :-- | :------- |
> | Highlight, underline, strikethrough | Colour noise, and weak for colour-blind readers | A callout, or bold for one term |
> | Footnotes | Readers jump away and lose their place | References at the end |
> | Embedding a whole page | It copies content, so changes go stale | A link to the page |
> | Tags typed in the text (#tag) | Tags live in properties | The tags property |
> | Horizontal lines | Folio already separates sections | A new section |
> | Diagrams written as code | They do not show the same in Folio | A picture of the diagram |
> | Raw HTML | It shows differently, or not at all | Plain Markdown |
> | Headings deeper than the template allows | Pages get hard to scan | Split the page |

## Before you send for review

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section, or keep a shorter copy for the new type. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Before you send for review
> Run through this list before you tell anyone the page is ready.
>
> - [ ] Summary filled in, one sentence.
> - [ ] Every [square bracket] replaced.
> - [ ] Every section of the template is there. Optional ones left out if they are empty.
> - [ ] Every picture has a caption.
> - [ ] Links work: click each one in Folio.
> - [ ] Grey notes deleted.
> - [ ] The **Check a page** AI prompt shows nothing left to fix.

## Using AI

%% Optional. Template builders: delete this section. %%

> [!guide]- Guide: Using AI
> Folio has four AI prompts under Admin > Templates > AI prompts. Each one copies with the template and the Format rules, so the AI follows the same rules as the format check.
>
> | Prompt | Use it when |
> | :-- | :------- |
> | Write a page | You have notes and want a first draft in the right layout, with properties filled in |
> | Fix a page | An older page needs moving into its template's layout |
> | Check a page | You want a list of what breaks the rules before you send a page for review |
> | Update this template | An Admin wants a template changed without breaking its notes |
>
> > [!warning] You are still the author
> > Check every fact the AI writes. It can sound sure and still be wrong. Folio never adds AI text to a page by itself.

## References

%% Core · Expects: link · Was: Sources. Every template ends with References. Keep it, and keep it last, unless a Video section follows. %%

- [[Format rules]]
- [[Help]]
- [Obsidian help: basic formatting](https://help.obsidian.md/syntax)

> [!guide]- Guide: References
> List the pages first, then outside sources. Give standards their edition and year: "NFPA 101, 2024 edition", not just "NFPA 101".

## Video

%% Optional. Optional sections can follow References. Keep a Video section only when good videos usually exist for the type. %%

- [Obsidian: creating links](https://help.obsidian.md/links)

> [!guide]- Guide: Video
> Link one good video at most. If there isn't one, delete the section rather than leaving it empty.

# Camera Placement

> [!abstract] Learning objectives
> - Choose a camera position from what the picture must show.
> - Avoid backlight and glare at doors.

## Start here

![[rack.png|inlL|240]]
A camera is placed for the question someone will ask later: who came through this door, and when. Start from the picture you need, then find the spot that gives it.

Put cameras at doors facing in, not out, so faces are lit by the room rather than the sky.

## Coverage levels

| Level | Can you | Use at |
|---|---|---|
| Detect | Tell something moved | Fence lines |
| Observe | See what a person is doing | Corridors |
| Recognise | Know someone you have met | Inside doors |
| Identify | Pick out a stranger | Entry points |

## Mistakes we see

> [!warning] Backlight
> A camera facing a glass door at noon shows a black shape. Move it or use a wide dynamic range camera.

- Mounted too high to see faces
- Pointed at a wall that was going to be a hallway
- Lens set to the wrong field of view after a layout change

# Cable Pathways

## Start here

Security cable runs in its own pathway from the device to the panel. Sharing with other trades causes the faults we spend days chasing.

## Rules

1. Conduit from the device box to above the ceiling.
2. Cable tray or J-hooks above the ceiling, every 1.5 m.
3. Conduit again into the security room.

## In the rack

![[before.png|inlR|240]]
Dress cable in the rack with velcro, never cable ties, and label both ends. A rack you can trace is a rack you can fix.

Leave a service loop at the panel, not at the device.
